questions.text: What is your date of termination or the date you left the employer?
questions.note: Anchors ESA limitation, HRC 1-year HRTO, 2-year civil limitation, EI ROE timing.

questions.text: What is your date of hire with this employer (or the earliest date you started working for them or a predecessor)?
questions.note: Used to calculate length of service for Bardal and ESA minimums.

questions.text: In which province did you primarily perform your work?
questions.note: Federal if ON + federally regulated industry. ESA/HRC apply to provincial employees.

questions.text: Was your employer in a federally regulated industry (e.g., banking, interprovincial transport, airline, telecom, broadcasting, federal crown corporation)?
questions.note: If YES → Canada Labour Code s.240 unjust dismissal; ESA does not apply. Flag for lawyer.

questions.text: Were you covered by a collective agreement or union at the time of termination?
questions.note: If unionized → civil courts have no jurisdiction (Weber v Ontario Hydro). Refer to grievance arbitration. End questionnaire.

questions.text: How were you formally classified by this employer?
questions.note: Classification affects notice rights. Dependent contractors get common law notice but not ESA.

questions.text: Were you labelled an 'independent contractor' or 'self-employed' but working exclusively or nearly exclusively for this employer?
questions.note: Sagaz / McKee / Keenan / Thurston. If near-exclusive engagement → likely dependent contractor or employee.

questions.text: Did you work for any other clients or employers during your engagement with this employer?
questions.note: Working for others weighs against dependent contractor status but does not rule it out if engagement was dominant.

questions.text: Did you sign a written employment agreement or offer letter?
questions.note: Written contract triggers termination clause analysis and entire-agreement clause review.

questions.text: Was your contract for a fixed end date (e.g., a 12-month contract), or ongoing/indefinite?
questions.note: Fixed term → Howard v Benson balance-of-term damages, no mitigation duty.

questions.text: Were you still within a probationary period at the time of termination?
questions.note: Probation triggers suitability standard, not just cause or Bardal. ESA minimums still apply after 3 months.

questions.text: How long was the probationary period stated in your contract or handbook?
questions.note: If >3 months and clause tries to exclude ESA, may void entire termination scheme via Waksdale.

questions.text: Were you terminated within that stated probationary period?
questions.note: If YES → employer must still show good-faith suitability assessment (Mison). Discrimination pretext possible.

questions.text: Does your written agreement contain a clause that limits or describes your entitlements on termination?
questions.note: If no clause or contract → common law Bardal applies automatically.

questions.text: Does the clause include a provision for termination 'for cause' or 'with cause'?
questions.note: Waksdale: if for-cause provision uses standard broader than ESA wilful misconduct → entire clause void.

questions.text: Does the for-cause provision use the exact phrase 'wilful misconduct' (matching the ESA standard), or does it use broader language such as 'just cause', 'cause', 'serious breach', or similar?
questions.note: If broader than wilful misconduct → Waksdale voids entire clause. Confirmed at SCC level 2025.

questions.text: Does the clause specify the amount of notice or pay in lieu you would receive on termination without cause?
questions.note: Specified amount must meet or exceed ESA minimum at all times (Machtinger; Rossman).

questions.text: Does the clause state that you receive only ESA minimums (i.e., no more than the statutory minimum)?
Does the clause include a provision stating that if any part conflicts with the ESA, the ESA applies (a 'saving clause')?
questions.note: Saving clauses cannot rehabilitate an illegal provision (Waksdale; Rossman; Tan v Stostac).

questions.text: Does the clause require continuation of your group benefits (health, dental, life insurance) during the notice period?
questions.note: Absence of benefits continuation renders clause void (Wood v Fred Deeley; North v Metaswitch).

questions.text: Does the clause contain any language permitting the employer to terminate your employment 'at any time' or 'at its sole discretion'?
questions.note: CURRENCY FLAG: Dufault doctrine. ONCA heard Baker/Jones Jan 16 2026. Decision pending. Strong demand-letter leverage; risky as sole SOC basis until ONCA rules.

questions.text: Does the clause address your rights in the event of constructive dismissal (i.e., fundamental change to your job)?
questions.note: If clause silent on constructive dismissal → common law Bardal applies to CD scenario.

questions.text: Was the contract (or the termination clause specifically) introduced after you had already started working, without any additional pay raise, bonus, or other benefit offered in exchange?
questions.note: Hobbs v TDI; Holland v Hostopia. Continued employment alone ≠ sufficient consideration for new restrictive term.

questions.text: Did you have an opportunity to obtain independent legal advice before signing the contract?
questions.note: Absence of ILA + grossly unfair terms supports unconscionability challenge (Titus v Cooke).

questions.text: How did your employment end?
questions.note: Determines which legal pathways are available.

questions.text: Did the employer state a specific reason for your termination?
Did the employer allege 'just cause' or 'cause' for your termination (i.e., claiming you did something that justified dismissal without any notice or pay)?
What reason(s) did the employer give for alleging cause?
Had the employer previously warned you, issued written discipline, or put you on a performance improvement plan before termination?
questions.note: Absence of progressive discipline supports finding that cause was not proportionate (McKinley contextual test).

questions.text: Did the employer ever condone the conduct they are now relying on as cause (i.e., knew about it but did not act)?
questions.note: Condonation defeats cause; also defeats after-acquired cause.

questions.text: Did the employer make any of the following changes to your job before you left? (Select all that apply)
questions.note: Potter Branch 1: unilateral act breaching essential term. Branch 2: cumulative conduct.

questions.text: Did the employer communicate this change to you in advance or give you any notice?
questions.note: Unilateral = no genuine consent obtained.

questions.text: Did you agree, in writing or by your conduct, to accept these changes and continue working?
questions.note: Acceptance/condonation may defeat CD claim. Must resign within reasonable time (Belton; Pham).

questions.text: How long after the change occurred did you continue to work before resigning or being terminated?
questions.note: Excessive delay may constitute condonation. Assessed contextually.

questions.text: Did the employer subject you to a pattern of conduct (rather than a single change) that made your workplace intolerable — such as persistent demeaning treatment, isolation, removal of responsibilities, or hostile management?
questions.note: Potter Branch 2: cumulative conduct demonstrating employer no longer intends to be bound.

questions.text: Was the pattern of conduct connected to a protected characteristic (e.g., related to your disability, age, sex, race, family status)?
questions.note: Connects constructive dismissal to HRC claim for Code damages.

questions.text: What was your age at the date your employment ended?
questions.note: Age >50 is significant Bardal elongating factor. Age >60 may support exceptional-circumstances notice beyond 24 months.

questions.text: What was your most recent job title?
questions.note: Used to assess character of employment.

questions.text: How would you best describe your role?
questions.note: Di Tomaso: character of employment of declining importance; no cap for unskilled workers.

questions.text: Did your role require specialized skills, certifications, or qualifications that are not widely available in the labour market?
questions.note: Specialized/non-transferable skills support longer notice; may support >24 months (Lynch v Avaya).

questions.text: Have you been able to find a comparable job since your termination?
questions.note: Difficulty finding work = adverse market conditions Bardal factor (Paquette v TeraGo).

questions.text: Are you in an industry that is currently experiencing layoffs, a downturn, or reduced hiring?
questions.note: Adverse sector conditions elongate notice (Paquette; Milwid IBM).

questions.text: Before joining this employer, were you employed in a stable, long-term job with another organization?
Did this employer (or someone acting on their behalf) reach out to recruit you — rather than you applying for the job?
questions.note: Active recruitment is the core inducement trigger.

questions.text: Were you promised any of the following during the recruitment process? (Select all that apply)
questions.note: Written promises → breach of contract and/or negligent misrep. Verbal → inducement/misrep.

questions.text: Were any of those promises made in writing (e.g., in the offer letter, an email, or a formal document)?
questions.note: Written = express contractual term or negligent/fraudulent misrepresentation. Stronger than verbal.

questions.text: Did you resign from your prior employer in order to accept this position?
questions.note: Resignation from prior = detrimental reliance anchor.

questions.text: Approximately how many years of service had you accumulated with your prior employer?
questions.note: Prior service used as experience factor (Addison/Manthadi); also grounds misrep reliance damages uncapped by notice.

questions.text: Did any of the promises made during recruitment turn out to be inaccurate, misleading, or not fulfilled?
questions.note: If YES and promises untrue at time made → negligent misrep (Cognos). If employer knew = fraudulent.

questions.text: Before this employer, did you work for a different employer doing the same or very similar work, in the same location or role?
questions.note: Addison/Manthadi/Chin: prior service = experience factor benefitting successor.

questions.text: Did this employer hire you directly from the predecessor — without any gap in your employment?
questions.note: No gap = strongest successor argument. ESA s.9 continuity if sale of business occurred.

questions.text: Was there any formal sale, purchase, or transfer of the business between the two employers (e.g., asset purchase, share purchase, contract assignment)?
questions.note: Abbott v Bombardier: sale of a specific bundle of tasks performed by identifiable group = ESA s.9 sale of business.

questions.text: Did the new employer expressly tell you that your prior service would NOT be recognized?
questions.note: Express negation reduces (but does not eliminate) experience credit under Antchipalovskaia/Manthadi.

questions.text: Were you paid any termination pay (notice pay or severance pay) when your employment ended?
Did your employer continue paying your benefits (health, dental, life insurance) for any period after termination?
questions.note: Benefits must continue during ESA notice period (ESA s.60).

questions.text: Were there any deductions taken from your final paycheque that you did not authorize in writing?
questions.note: ESA s.13: unauthorized deductions prohibited. Cash shortages categorically prohibited s.13(5).

questions.text: Were you paid out all accrued and unused vacation pay on termination?
questions.note: ESA ss.33-41: vacation pay must be paid on termination.

questions.text: Were you regularly working more than 44 hours per week without overtime pay?
questions.note: ESA s.22: overtime at 1.5x after 44 hours. Manager exemption strictly construed.

questions.text: Has your employer issued your Record of Employment (ROE)?
questions.note: ROE required within 5 calendar days of end of pay period.

questions.text: Was the reason for separation coded correctly on your ROE? (For example: 'A' = shortage of work; 'M' = dismissal; 'E' = quit)
questions.note: False ROE code = Honda/aggravated damages trigger + EI Act s.38/39 penalty exposure for employer.

questions.text: Were you laid off (rather than terminated) at any point during your employment?
questions.note: Layoff >13 weeks in 20-week period (or >35 weeks with benefits) = deemed termination.

questions.text: Were at least 50 other employees also terminated around the same time at your workplace?
questions.note: ESA s.58 mass termination: 8-16 weeks enhanced notice; Form 1 required; clock starts only on filing.

questions.text: Do you believe your termination or any adverse treatment at work was connected to any of the following characteristics?
questions.note: Moore v BC Education: protected characteristic need only be a factor, not the sole cause.

questions.text: Please describe the adverse treatment you experienced and how you believe it was connected to that characteristic.
Did you have a disability or medical condition that your employer was aware of?
Did you request any accommodation from your employer related to your disability or medical condition?
questions.note: Failure to even inquire = Code violation (Lane v ADGA).

questions.text: Did your employer deny, delay, or fail to adequately provide that accommodation?
questions.note: Must exhaust accommodation before frustration claim (Naccarato v Costco).

questions.text: Were you subjected to workplace harassment — repeated vexatious comments or conduct — that you believe was connected to a protected characteristic?
questions.note: Section 5(2): poisoned workplace. Assessed objectively. Single egregious incident may suffice.

questions.text: Were you subjected to any sexual harassment or unwanted sexual solicitation or advances?
questions.note: s.7: personal liability of harasser possible; potential for significant IDFS damages ($75K-$200K+).

questions.text: Did you complain to HR, a manager, or any authority about the harassment or discrimination you experienced?
questions.note: Complaint triggers reprisal protection under s.8.

questions.text: Did adverse treatment (discipline, demotion, termination, change in duties) occur after or shortly after you made that complaint?
questions.note: Temporal proximity supports reprisal inference.

questions.text: Were you pregnant, on parental/pregnancy leave, or planning to take such leave around the time of your termination?
questions.note: Termination during/after pregnancy/parental leave = strong presumption of Code violation.

questions.text: Do you have childcare or eldercare responsibilities that made it difficult for you to meet a workplace requirement (e.g., schedule, location, overtime)?
questions.note: Ontario applies Misetich test (Moore analysis). Federal applies Johnstone test.

questions.text: Have you filed or are you considering filing an application with the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario (HRTO)?
questions.note: CRITICAL: Filing at HRTO may bar civil action on same facts (s.34(11)). Must resolve before filing either.

questions.text: Describe how the termination meeting or dismissal occurred.
questions.note: Honda v Keays: candid, reasonable, honest, forthright standard.

questions.text: Did the employer make any of the following claims or take any of the following actions at or after termination? (Select all that apply)
questions.note: Each checked item is a potential Honda and/or punitive damages trigger.

questions.text: Have you experienced any of the following as a result of the termination or the manner in which it occurred? (Select all that apply)
questions.note: Krmpotic 2024 ONCA: lay evidence of anxiety/sleep disturbance suffices; no medical evidence strictly required.

questions.text: Did the employer make a false or misleading allegation of serious misconduct (e.g., theft, fraud, harassment) as a reason for your termination?
questions.note: False cause allegations = classic Honda trigger; if persisted through trial = punitive (Doyle v Zochem).

questions.text: Did the employer threaten or bring legal proceedings against you (e.g., counterclaim, threat of lawsuit, referral to police) that appear to be retaliatory?
questions.note: Tactical/retaliatory counterclaim or complaint = punitive damages trigger (Ruston v Keddco; Pate Estate).

questions.text: What was your annual base salary at the time of termination?
Did your compensation include a bonus (annual, performance, sign-on, retention)?
questions.note: Matthews v Ocean Nutrition: bonus during notice period recoverable unless unambiguously excluded.

questions.text: Does your contract or bonus plan state that you must be 'actively employed' at the time of payment to receive the bonus?
questions.note: Matthews: active-employment clauses generally insufficient to exclude bonus during notice period.

questions.text: Did you hold stock options, RSUs, LTIP units, or other equity-based compensation?
questions.note: O'Reilly; Battiston; Manastersky; Andros; Celestini. Same Matthews two-step applies.

questions.text: Did you have to click-through or sign equity plan documents online without those plans being specifically highlighted or explained to you?
questions.note: Battiston 2021 ONCA: conscious annual click-through may be sufficient acceptance. Lawyer review required.

questions.text: Did your compensation include any of the following? (Select all that apply)
questions.note: All compensation components form part of damages (Matthews para 49; Wallace).

questions.text: Did the employer owe you any commission, draw, or variable pay that was unpaid at termination?
Did you have a signing bonus or retention bonus that the employer is attempting to claw back?
questions.note: ESA s.13 prohibition on unauthorized deductions; penalty doctrine; restraint of trade analysis.

questions.text: Does your employment agreement contain a non-competition clause (restricting you from working for competitors)?
Was the non-competition clause signed on or after October 25, 2021?
questions.note: ESA s.67.2: non-competes signed on/after Oct 25 2021 are void (subject to sale-of-business and executive exceptions).

questions.text: At the time you signed the non-compete, were you a 'C-Suite' executive (CEO, COO, CFO, CIO, CLO, CHRO, or similar chief officer)?
questions.note: Executive exception to ESA s.67.2 ban: C-suite officers may be bound by non-competes post-Oct 2021.

questions.text: Does your agreement contain a non-solicitation clause (restricting you from contacting clients or employees)?
questions.note: Non-solicitation clauses not banned by ESA s.67.2; common-law reasonableness test applies.

questions.text: Is the employer threatening to enforce any restrictive covenant against you, or seeking damages for an alleged breach?
Did you raise a workplace health and safety concern with your employer, a supervisor, or the Ministry of Labour before your termination?
questions.note: OHSA s.50 reprisal: reverse onus on employer. Reinstatement + back pay available.

questions.text: Did you refuse to perform unsafe work under OHSA s.43 before your termination?
questions.note: Work refusal = protected activity under OHSA s.43; reprisal prohibited s.50.

questions.text: Were you a Joint Health and Safety Committee member or a Health and Safety Representative?
questions.note: JHSC role = additional OHSA protection.

questions.text: Did you experience or witness workplace violence or threats of violence?
questions.note: OHSA ss.32.0.1-32.0.7: violence prevention duties; s.32.0.5(3)-(4): disclosure obligation for violent-history persons.

questions.text: Were you subjected to workplace harassment as defined under OHSA — repeated vexatious comment or conduct — and did you report it?
questions.note: OHSA ss.32.0.6-32.0.7: employer must investigate and report results. Failure grounds constructive dismissal.

questions.text: Were you on a disability, medical, pregnancy, parental, or any other statutory leave when you were terminated?
questions.note: Termination during protected leave = ESA s.53 + Code violation presumption.

questions.text: Did you sign a release or severance agreement when your employment ended?
questions.note: Release may be challenged on unconscionability (Titus v Cooke): grossly unfair terms + no ILA + pressure.

questions.text: When you signed the release, were you given adequate time to review it (e.g., at least a few days), and did you receive independent legal advice?
questions.note: No ILA + immediate pressure = strong unconscionability indicator (Rubin v Home Depot).

questions.text: Is the employer a corporation that may be insolvent, or is there a concern about collecting any judgment?
questions.note: ESA s.81 / OBCA s.131: directors personally liable for up to 6 months wages + 12 months vacation.

questions.text: Is this a situation where you believe a related company or common employer (not just the named employer) is also responsible?
questions.note: Downtown Eatery / King v Danbury: common employer doctrine — degree of legal commonality test.

questions.text: Has your employer made any statements to industry contacts, clients, or former colleagues about the reasons for your departure that you believe are inaccurate or damaging?
questions.note: Defamatory statements post-dismissal = tort + Honda damages trigger.

questions.text: Since your termination, have you been actively looking for work?
questions.note: Red Deer College: burden on employer to prove failure to mitigate.

questions.text: Have you found any new employment since your termination?
questions.note: Income earned during notice period is deductible (Sylvester v BC).

questions.text: If yes, when did you start the new job, and what is your new annual compensation?
questions.note: Quantifies income differential; commute/other costs may be special damages.

questions.text: Did your former employer offer to reinstate you or offer you continued employment after your termination?
questions.note: Evans v Teamsters: may be required to accept if offer genuine, comparable, not hostile/humiliating.

questions.text: Have you received Employment Insurance (EI) benefits since your termination?
questions.note: EI not deducted from damages (Jack Cewe v Jorgenson); employer must withhold/remit on settlement (EI Act s.46).

questions.text: Did you receive any CERB, CRB, or other COVID-era government income support?
questions.note: CURRENCY FLAG: Ontario courts generally do NOT deduct CERB (Iriotakis; Fogelman). No SCC ruling. Yates (BCCA); Oostlander (ABCA) also not deducting.

questions.text: Is there anything else about your employment or termination that you believe is relevant and has not been covered?
questions.note: Open field for lawyer review. May surface additional issues.

Resigned due to intolerable changes (constructive dismissal)
Contract ended due to illness / impossibility

Harassment or misconduct toward a colleague

OPT_CD_CHANGES.label: Pay cut or reduction in compensation
Required to move to a different work location
Material change in hours or schedule
Required to attend office after remote-work arrangement
Removal from projects, team, or communications

OPT_RECRUIT_PROMISES.label: Long-term job security or stable employment
Opportunity to build, lead, or grow a team or division
Supervision by a qualified professional for credential advancement

OPT_BAD_FAITH_ACTS.label: Falsely alleged serious misconduct (e.g. theft, fraud, harassment)
Issued ROE with incorrect reason for separation
Promised benefits would continue but cut them off
Delayed or withheld final pay or termination pay
Made damaging statements about you to others
Paid nothing or less than ESA minimums
Filed or threatened a lawsuit against you
Made a complaint to police or regulator without legitimate basis
Conducted a sham or inadequate investigation

OPT_DISTRESS_SYMPTOMS.label: Difficulty obtaining Employment Insurance due to false ROE
